title: A single unattached chromosome can hold up a whole cell division

cover.alt: A grey, flat cell seen under a phase-contrast microscope, with dark, threadlike chromosomes gathered near its centre.
cover.credit: Stout J, Rizk R, Kline S, Walczak C · CC BY 2.0

body: Before a cell divides, each chromosome has been copied into two joined sister chromatids. They line up across the middle of the cell, and fibres of the spindle must grab every pair from opposite sides. A safety system, the **spindle checkpoint**, stops the cell from pulling the sisters apart until each pair is properly attached: even one unattached chromosome gives off a 'wait' signal that holds back the split. When this goes wrong, daughter cells can end up with the wrong number of chromosomes, a state called aneuploidy that is common in cancer cells.

slides.alt: Under a microscope, dark chromosomes in a flat grey cell gather into a band across its middle, split into two sets that move apart, and the cell pinches into two.
slides.caption: Time-lapse of a rat kangaroo kidney cell dividing, about 34 minutes in 11 seconds: chromosomes gather in a band across the middle, split into two sets, and the cell pinches in two.
slides.credit: Stout J, Rizk R, Kline S, Walczak C · CC BY 2.0 · excerpt

slides.heading: Put the stages of mitosis in order
slides.explanation: A safety system, the spindle checkpoint, guards the step from metaphase, when chromosomes line up, to anaphase, when each one’s two copies are pulled apart.

left.label: Checkpoint working
left.text: The split waits until every chromosome is attached to both ends of the spindle, so each new cell gets a full set.

right.label: Checkpoint failing
right.text: Chromosomes can be shared out unevenly, leaving cells with too many or too few. This is common in human tumours.

slides.heading: A favourite cell to watch
slides.text: The cell in the clip is a PtK cell, from the kidney of a rat kangaroo, the long-nosed potoroo. Biologists like these cells for filming mitosis because they stay large and flat and have a small number of big chromosomes.

slides.question: What does a chromosome that is not yet attached to the spindle do?
options: Sends a signal that delays the split
slides.explanation: Unattached chromosomes produce a 'wait' signal. As early as 1970, a lagging chromosome was seen to postpone the split until minutes after it reached the middle.
